source: CRI FS AI RMF Guidebook v1.0

adoption_stages.name: Scoping
adoption_stages.description: Organization is determining if and how AI applies to its operations, products, and services. Focus is on identifying AI use cases, understanding regulatory expectations, and establishing initial governance structures.

adoption_stages.name: Minimum Viable
adoption_stages.description: Basic controls are in place for initial AI use. The organization has established foundational policies, assigned responsibilities, and implemented minimum risk management practices sufficient for limited AI deployment.

adoption_stages.name: Scaling
adoption_stages.description: The organization is expanding AI use with more mature controls. Processes are repeatable, metrics are tracked, and governance structures support multiple AI initiatives across business lines.

adoption_stages.name: Full Implementation
adoption_stages.description: Comprehensive controls are in place for a mature AI program. The organization has enterprise-wide AI governance, continuous monitoring, advanced risk management, and robust accountability mechanisms integrated into the three lines of defense.

controls.objective_text: The organization maintains an inventory of all applicable AI-related laws, regulations, and supervisory guidance (e.g., SR 11-7, OCC 2011-12, EU AI Act, state-level AI statutes) and maps them to AI systems in use.
controls.implementation_guidance: Establish a regulatory tracking process that identifies new and updated AI-related requirements. Assign ownership to legal/compliance for maintaining the inventory. Map each regulation to affected AI systems and business lines. Review quarterly and after any regulatory publication.
controls.risk_statement: Failure to track regulatory requirements may result in non-compliance, supervisory action, enforcement orders, or consent decrees from banking regulators.

controls.objective_text: AI governance policies explicitly address requirements from prudential regulators, including the OCC, Federal Reserve, FDIC, and CFPB, as well as industry-specific standards such as FFIEC guidance.
controls.implementation_guidance: Draft AI governance policies that reference specific regulatory expectations. Include provisions for model risk management per SR 11-7, fair lending per ECOA/Reg B, and consumer protection per UDAAP. Ensure board-level approval of policies.
controls.risk_statement: Generic AI policies that do not address financial services regulatory specifics create gaps in compliance coverage and increase examination risk.

controls.objective_text: The organization monitors proposed rulemaking, supervisory statements, and interagency guidance related to AI and updates its compliance program proactively.
controls.implementation_guidance: Subscribe to Federal Register notices, OCC bulletins, Fed supervision letters, and CFPB advisory opinions. Assign a regulatory change management function to assess impact of proposed rules on AI systems. Conduct gap analyses within 60 days of final rule publication.
controls.risk_statement: Reactive compliance posture leads to rushed implementations, control gaps, and potential MRA/MRIA findings during examinations.

controls.objective_text: The organization maintains a tiered AI risk classification framework that categorizes AI systems by risk level (e.g., critical, high, medium, low) based on impact to consumers, safety, and financial stability.
controls.implementation_guidance: Define risk tiers aligned with SR 11-7 model tiering. Consider factors such as consumer impact, financial materiality, operational criticality, and reputational risk. Assign tier-specific control requirements. Review classifications annually or upon material change.
controls.risk_statement: Without risk-based tiering, the organization may over-invest in low-risk AI while under-managing high-risk systems that could cause consumer harm or systemic issues.

controls.objective_text: AI risk classification explicitly considers fair lending implications, BSA/AML exposure, and consumer protection risks as elevated risk factors for financial services AI systems.
controls.implementation_guidance: Include fair lending, BSA/AML, and UDAAP risk as mandatory evaluation criteria in the AI risk tiering methodology. Systems used in credit decisioning, fraud detection, or customer-facing interactions should receive heightened scrutiny regardless of technical complexity.
controls.risk_statement: AI systems that affect consumer access to financial products carry outsized regulatory and reputational risk that generic tiering frameworks may underweight.

controls.objective_text: The risk classification framework is reviewed and approved by the model risk management function and aligned with the organization's enterprise risk appetite statement.
controls.implementation_guidance: Ensure MRM (Model Risk Management) validates the AI risk tiering methodology. Align AI risk appetite with board-approved enterprise risk appetite. Document how AI risk classifications feed into enterprise risk reporting and capital planning.
controls.risk_statement: Disconnected AI risk classification from enterprise risk management creates blind spots in board reporting and capital adequacy assessments.

controls.objective_text: The organization defines and documents acceptable AI use boundaries, including explicit prohibitions on AI applications that conflict with fair lending laws, consumer protection requirements, or safety-and-soundness standards.
controls.implementation_guidance: Publish an AI acceptable use policy that specifies permitted and prohibited use cases. Prohibit autonomous credit decisioning without human review for high-risk decisions. Define guardrails for generative AI in customer communications. Review annually with legal and compliance.
controls.risk_statement: Absence of defined AI use boundaries leads to ad hoc deployments that may violate regulatory expectations or cause consumer harm.

controls.objective_text: AI use boundaries address the use of generative AI for financial advice, investment recommendations, and insurance underwriting, with specific controls for hallucination risk and unauthorized practice.
controls.implementation_guidance: Establish specific policies for GenAI in customer-facing financial contexts. Require human review of any AI-generated financial advice. Implement output filtering to prevent unauthorized investment or insurance recommendations. Document legal review of GenAI customer interactions.
controls.risk_statement: Uncontrolled generative AI in financial advisory contexts risks regulatory violation under the Investment Advisers Act, state insurance laws, and FINRA rules.

controls.objective_text: Processes exist to evaluate and approve new AI use cases against defined boundaries before development begins, including assessment of regulatory implications by compliance and legal functions.
controls.implementation_guidance: Implement an AI use case intake process requiring compliance, legal, and risk sign-off before development. Use a standardized assessment template covering regulatory requirements, consumer impact, and risk tier. Maintain an approval log auditable by examiners.
controls.risk_statement: Developing AI systems without pre-approval creates compliance risks that are costly to remediate post-deployment and may draw supervisory criticism.

controls.objective_text: The organization establishes an AI ethics framework that addresses fairness, transparency, accountability, and consumer protection in alignment with regulatory expectations for financial institutions.
controls.implementation_guidance: Develop an AI ethics framework endorsed by senior management. Address bias and fairness in lending and insurance. Include principles for transparency in AI-driven decisions that affect consumers. Align with OCC heightened standards and CFPB expectations on algorithmic fairness.
controls.risk_statement: Financial institutions without an AI ethics framework face reputational risk and regulatory scrutiny, particularly from the CFPB on algorithmic fairness.

controls.objective_text: The AI ethics framework is operationalized through defined processes for ethical review of AI systems, including standing ethics review boards or committees with cross-functional representation.
controls.implementation_guidance: Establish an AI ethics review committee with representatives from risk, compliance, legal, business lines, and technology. Define triggers for ethical review (e.g., consumer-facing AI, credit decisions, surveillance). Document review outcomes and remediation actions.
controls.risk_statement: Ethics frameworks without operational processes remain aspirational and fail to prevent harmful AI deployments in practice.

controls.objective_text: Ethical considerations specific to financial services are documented, including the ethical implications of AI in credit access, wealth management, fraud detection, and employment decisions within the institution.
controls.implementation_guidance: Document domain-specific ethical considerations for each major AI use case category. Address disparate impact in credit and insurance. Consider surveillance ethics in fraud/AML monitoring. Evaluate employee impact of AI-driven workforce decisions. Review annually.
controls.risk_statement: Generic AI ethics policies miss the unique ethical dimensions of financial services, such as AI's potential to perpetuate redlining patterns or exclude underbanked populations.

controls.objective_text: The organization defines and enforces minimum technical standards for AI system development, testing, deployment, and monitoring, consistent with model risk management expectations under SR 11-7.
controls.implementation_guidance: Publish AI technical standards covering development lifecycle, code review, testing requirements, deployment gates, and monitoring. Align with SR 11-7 expectations for model development, implementation, and use. Include standards for data management, version control, and reproducibility.
controls.risk_statement: Inconsistent technical standards across AI initiatives lead to quality issues, deployment failures, and examination findings on model risk management.

controls.objective_text: Technical standards address the unique risks of third-party and open-source AI models, including foundation models, with requirements for evaluation, customization controls, and ongoing monitoring.
controls.implementation_guidance: Define standards for evaluating third-party AI models before adoption. Require documentation of model provenance, training data characteristics, and known limitations. Establish controls for fine-tuning and prompt engineering of foundation models. Monitor vendor model updates for drift.
controls.risk_statement: Adopting third-party AI models without technical due diligence introduces uncontrolled model risk and potential intellectual property or data privacy issues.

controls.objective_text: Technical standards include requirements for AI system documentation sufficient to support independent model validation, regulatory examination, and audit review.
controls.implementation_guidance: Require comprehensive model documentation including purpose, methodology, data sources, assumptions, limitations, performance metrics, and validation results. Ensure documentation meets SR 11-7 standards for effective challenge. Maintain documentation in a centralized, version-controlled repository.
controls.risk_statement: Insufficient AI documentation impedes independent validation and examination, resulting in MRA findings and potential restrictions on model use.

controls.objective_text: The organization maintains an enterprise-wide AI system inventory (model inventory) that is complete, accurate, and includes all AI/ML models regardless of development source, consistent with SR 11-7 model inventory requirements.
controls.implementation_guidance: Implement a centralized AI/model inventory system. Include all models: internally developed, vendor-provided, open-source, and embedded in third-party products. Capture metadata including risk tier, owner, validation status, deployment status, and regulatory scope. Update inventory in real-time or at minimum quarterly.
controls.risk_statement: Incomplete model inventories are a recurring examination finding and prevent effective oversight of AI risk across the enterprise.

controls.objective_text: The AI inventory captures sufficient metadata to support risk-based oversight, including model purpose, risk tier, data sensitivity classification, consumer impact assessment, and regulatory applicability.
controls.implementation_guidance: Define mandatory inventory fields aligned with SR 11-7 and internal risk framework. Include: model name, owner, business line, risk tier, validation date, performance metrics, data sources, regulatory scope, and consumer impact rating. Enable filtering and reporting by any field combination.
controls.risk_statement: An inventory without adequate metadata cannot support risk-based prioritization, leaving high-risk AI systems under-monitored.

controls.objective_text: Processes ensure that AI systems embedded in vendor products, fintech partnerships, and third-party platforms are identified and included in the AI inventory with appropriate risk assessment.
controls.implementation_guidance: Integrate AI discovery into vendor management and procurement processes. Require vendors to disclose AI/ML components in their products via contractual provisions. Assess embedded AI against the same risk framework as internally developed models. Flag shadow AI use through technology governance controls.
controls.risk_statement: Vendor-embedded AI that escapes inventory creates unmonitored model risk and may violate regulatory expectations for comprehensive model governance.

controls.objective_text: The organization establishes AI-specific incident response and escalation procedures integrated with existing operational risk and business continuity frameworks.
controls.implementation_guidance: Develop AI incident response playbooks covering model failures, data breaches, bias events, and adversarial attacks. Define severity levels with corresponding response times and escalation paths. Integrate with enterprise incident management and business continuity planning. Include regulatory notification requirements.
controls.risk_statement: AI system failures without predefined response procedures lead to prolonged outages, consumer harm, and delayed regulatory notifications.

controls.objective_text: AI incident response procedures include defined triggers for regulatory notification, including materiality thresholds aligned with OCC, FDIC, and state regulatory reporting requirements.
controls.implementation_guidance: Map AI incident types to regulatory notification requirements. Define materiality thresholds for reporting to the OCC (e.g., significant operational disruption), state regulators (data breach notification), and the CFPB (consumer harm). Establish maximum time-to-notify aligned with regulatory expectations. Conduct tabletop exercises annually.
controls.risk_statement: Failure to timely notify regulators of material AI incidents can result in enforcement action and loss of supervisory trust.

controls.objective_text: Post-incident review processes are established for AI system failures, including root cause analysis, lessons learned, and control remediation tracked to completion.
controls.implementation_guidance: Require post-incident reviews for all AI incidents above a defined severity threshold. Conduct root cause analysis within 30 days. Document lessons learned and share across AI teams. Track remediation actions to closure with second-line oversight. Report trends to the risk committee quarterly.
controls.risk_statement: Without structured post-incident review, the organization fails to learn from AI failures and repeats preventable incidents.

controls.objective_text: Roles and responsibilities for AI risk management are clearly defined across the three lines of defense, with the first line owning AI systems, the second line providing independent oversight, and the third line providing assurance.
controls.implementation_guidance: Document AI-specific responsibilities for each line of defense. First line: model development, implementation, ongoing monitoring. Second line (MRM, compliance): independent validation, policy setting, risk assessment. Third line (internal audit): assurance over AI governance effectiveness. Define RACI matrices for key AI processes.
controls.risk_statement: Ambiguous AI responsibilities across defense lines lead to control gaps, duplicated effort, or inadequate independent oversight — a common examination criticism.

controls.objective_text: A senior executive (e.g., Chief AI Officer, Chief Data Officer, or Chief Risk Officer) is designated with enterprise-wide accountability for AI risk management and governance.
controls.implementation_guidance: Assign a named senior executive with authority and accountability for AI governance. Define reporting lines to the board risk committee. Ensure the role has sufficient independence, resources, and organizational stature. Document the designation in governance policies and communicate to regulators.
controls.risk_statement: Without clear senior executive ownership, AI governance lacks authority and accountability, resulting in fragmented oversight across business lines.

controls.objective_text: AI system owners are formally designated for each AI system in the inventory, with documented accountability for risk management, performance, and compliance throughout the model lifecycle.
controls.implementation_guidance: Require formal designation of a model/system owner for each AI system at registration. Define owner responsibilities including ongoing monitoring, issue remediation, validation coordination, and regulatory response. Ensure owners have sufficient technical understanding to fulfill accountability. Review ownership assignments annually.
controls.risk_statement: Unowned AI systems drift without accountability, accumulating risk through unmonitored performance degradation and unresolved issues.

controls.objective_text: The organization conducts AI-specific skills assessments and maintains training programs to ensure staff across all three lines of defense have competency appropriate to their AI responsibilities.
controls.implementation_guidance: Assess AI literacy needs by role (developers, validators, compliance officers, auditors, executives). Develop tiered training programs from AI awareness to advanced technical skills. Track completion and competency assessment results. Require recertification annually. Budget for external training and conferences.
controls.risk_statement: Insufficient AI competency across defense lines leads to ineffective development, validation, and oversight — a known driver of model risk events.

controls.objective_text: Model risk management and internal audit functions maintain sufficient expertise in AI/ML techniques to provide effective challenge and assurance over AI systems.
controls.implementation_guidance: Hire or develop AI/ML specialists within MRM and audit functions. Ensure validators can independently assess model methodology, data quality, and performance. Provide audit staff with training on AI-specific risks and controls. Supplement with qualified third-party specialists where internal expertise is insufficient.
controls.risk_statement: Second and third line functions lacking AI expertise cannot provide effective challenge, undermining the three lines of defense model for AI.

controls.objective_text: Board members and senior executives receive regular AI literacy training sufficient to exercise informed oversight of AI strategy, risks, and governance.
controls.implementation_guidance: Provide at minimum annual AI education sessions for the board and executive committee. Cover AI capabilities, limitations, risks, regulatory landscape, and the organization's AI strategy. Use case studies relevant to financial services. Assess board comprehension and adjust content accordingly.
controls.risk_statement: Boards lacking AI understanding cannot exercise meaningful oversight, resulting in rubber-stamp approvals and inadequate strategic direction.

controls.objective_text: The board of directors or a designated board committee receives regular reporting on AI risk exposure, governance effectiveness, and material AI incidents, with sufficient detail to exercise oversight.
controls.implementation_guidance: Establish quarterly AI risk reporting to the board risk committee. Include: AI inventory summary, risk tier distribution, validation status, open issues, performance metrics, incidents, and emerging risks. Provide trend analysis and comparison to risk appetite. Ensure reports are actionable and not purely informational.
controls.risk_statement: Inadequate board reporting on AI risk impairs governance and may result in examination findings on board oversight effectiveness.

controls.objective_text: Senior management AI governance committees meet regularly with defined charters, membership requirements, and decision-making authority over AI strategy, risk acceptance, and resource allocation.
controls.implementation_guidance: Establish an AI governance committee with a formal charter. Define membership to include CRO, CDO/CAIO, business line heads, compliance, legal, and technology leadership. Meet at minimum monthly. Document decisions, action items, and escalations. Report to the board committee quarterly.
controls.risk_statement: AI governance without a structured committee process leads to inconsistent decision-making and inadequate senior management engagement.

controls.objective_text: Internal audit includes AI governance and model risk management within its audit universe, with risk-based audit planning that covers the full AI lifecycle.
controls.implementation_guidance: Include AI governance, MRM, and individual high-risk AI systems in the audit universe. Develop a risk-based audit plan that covers AI strategy, development practices, validation, monitoring, and third-party AI. Execute AI audits using staff with appropriate AI expertise. Report findings to the audit committee.
controls.risk_statement: Excluding AI from the audit universe leaves governance effectiveness unassured and may result in regulatory criticism of audit coverage.

controls.objective_text: The organization integrates AI risk into its enterprise risk management framework, with AI-specific risk categories, appetite statements, and reporting aligned with existing operational, compliance, and strategic risk processes.
controls.implementation_guidance: Extend the ERM taxonomy to include AI-specific risk categories (model risk, algorithmic bias, AI operational risk). Define AI risk appetite metrics and thresholds approved by the board. Integrate AI risk reporting into enterprise risk dashboards. Align AI risk assessment methodology with existing ERM processes.
controls.risk_statement: Siloed AI risk management disconnected from ERM creates blind spots in enterprise risk reporting and may understate aggregate risk exposure.

controls.objective_text: AI risk appetite and tolerance levels are defined, quantified where possible, and approved by the board, with clear escalation procedures when tolerances are breached.
controls.implementation_guidance: Define quantitative AI risk appetite metrics (e.g., maximum model risk losses, bias thresholds, system availability). Set tolerance levels with escalation triggers. Monitor metrics continuously against thresholds. Escalate breaches per defined procedures. Review appetite annually or after material events.
controls.risk_statement: Undefined AI risk appetite means the organization cannot objectively determine whether AI risk is within acceptable bounds.

controls.objective_text: AI risk assessments consider interconnections between AI systems and critical financial infrastructure, including payment systems, clearing houses, and SIFMUs.
controls.implementation_guidance: Map AI system dependencies on critical financial infrastructure. Assess concentration risk where multiple AI systems depend on shared infrastructure or data sources. Evaluate systemic risk implications of AI failures in market-critical functions. Include interconnection analysis in risk assessments for high-tier AI systems.
controls.risk_statement: Ignoring AI interconnections with critical infrastructure could contribute to systemic risk events that affect financial stability.

controls.objective_text: The organization establishes AI-specific policies and procedures that are reviewed at least annually, approved by appropriate governance bodies, and communicated to all relevant personnel.
controls.implementation_guidance: Maintain a policy framework covering AI governance, development standards, validation, monitoring, third-party AI, and acceptable use. Require annual review and approval by the AI governance committee. Version-control all policies. Distribute to relevant personnel with acknowledgment tracking. Align with enterprise policy management standards.
controls.risk_statement: Outdated or poorly communicated AI policies lead to inconsistent practices and examination findings on governance effectiveness.

controls.objective_text: AI policies address the full model lifecycle from ideation through decommissioning, with specific requirements for each phase aligned with SR 11-7 expectations.
controls.implementation_guidance: Define policy requirements for each lifecycle phase: use case approval, development standards, validation, implementation, ongoing monitoring, change management, and decommissioning. Specify gate criteria for progression between phases. Require documentation at each stage. Align with SR 11-7 lifecycle management expectations.
controls.risk_statement: Lifecycle gaps in AI policy coverage allow AI systems to bypass controls at critical transition points, increasing risk.

controls.objective_text: Exception management processes exist for AI policy deviations, with risk-based approval authority, time-bound remediation plans, and second-line oversight.
controls.implementation_guidance: Define an exception process for AI policy deviations. Require risk assessment of each exception. Assign approval authority based on risk level (e.g., CRO for high-risk exceptions). Set maximum exception duration with mandatory remediation plans. Track exceptions centrally. Report to governance committee quarterly.
controls.risk_statement: Unmanaged policy exceptions accumulate risk and undermine the governance framework, potentially creating systemic control weaknesses.

controls.objective_text: The organization allocates sufficient budget, staff, and technology resources to support AI risk management activities proportionate to the scale and complexity of its AI program.
controls.implementation_guidance: Conduct annual resource needs assessment for AI risk management. Budget for MRM staffing, validation tools, monitoring infrastructure, and training. Benchmark resource levels against peer institutions and regulatory expectations. Ensure resource allocation is approved by senior management and reported to the board.
controls.risk_statement: Under-resourced AI risk management cannot keep pace with AI deployment, creating a growing gap between AI use and oversight capacity.

controls.objective_text: Resource allocation for AI validation and monitoring scales with the AI inventory, ensuring that validation backlogs do not create unacceptable risk exposure from unvalidated models in production.
controls.implementation_guidance: Track validation backlog as a key risk metric. Define maximum acceptable time-to-validation by risk tier. Allocate MRM resources to maintain backlog within tolerance. Use risk-based prioritization to sequence validation work. Escalate capacity constraints to governance committee when backlogs exceed thresholds.
controls.risk_statement: Validation backlogs leave AI systems operating without independent challenge, a primary driver of model risk events in financial services.

controls.objective_text: The organization invests in AI risk management tooling, including model monitoring platforms, bias detection tools, and documentation repositories, to enable scalable AI governance.
controls.implementation_guidance: Evaluate and implement AI governance technology including model monitoring, experiment tracking, bias analysis, and documentation management. Prioritize tools that support regulatory reporting requirements. Ensure tooling is accessible to all three lines of defense. Conduct build-vs-buy analysis for key capabilities.
controls.risk_statement: Manual AI governance processes do not scale, leading to monitoring gaps and inconsistent control execution as the AI program grows.

controls.objective_text: The organization maintains competency requirements for AI roles, including model developers, data engineers, validators, and AI risk managers, with hiring practices that attract qualified talent.
controls.implementation_guidance: Define competency frameworks for AI-related roles. Require minimum qualifications for model developers (statistics, ML, programming) and validators (independent technical capability). Develop competitive compensation packages. Establish partnerships with universities and AI research institutions for talent pipeline.
controls.risk_statement: Inability to attract and retain qualified AI talent leads to quality issues in development, validation gaps, and reliance on unqualified staff.

controls.objective_text: Staff involved in AI development, deployment, and oversight receive role-specific training on financial services regulations, ethical AI practices, and the organization's AI governance framework.
controls.implementation_guidance: Develop mandatory training curricula differentiated by role. Include regulatory context (SR 11-7, fair lending, BSA/AML) for all AI staff. Provide ethics training with financial services scenarios. Require governance framework training for new hires. Track completion and assess effectiveness annually.
controls.risk_statement: Technical AI staff without regulatory and governance training may develop systems that are technically sound but non-compliant or ethically problematic.

controls.objective_text: Succession planning and knowledge management processes ensure continuity of AI expertise, preventing single points of failure in critical AI system ownership and oversight.
controls.implementation_guidance: Identify key-person dependencies for critical AI systems. Develop succession plans for AI leadership and system owners. Implement knowledge management practices including comprehensive documentation, code comments, and cross-training. Ensure at least two qualified individuals can support each critical AI system.
controls.risk_statement: Key-person dependency in AI creates operational risk when staff depart, potentially leaving critical systems without qualified oversight.

controls.objective_text: AI governance processes are integrated with existing enterprise change management, SDLC, and IT governance frameworks to avoid duplication and ensure consistent control execution.
controls.implementation_guidance: Map AI governance gates to existing SDLC phases. Integrate AI risk assessment into enterprise change management. Align AI documentation requirements with IT governance standards. Use existing ticketing and workflow systems for AI governance activities where possible. Avoid creating parallel processes.
controls.risk_statement: Siloed AI governance creates confusion, duplication, and process fatigue that undermines compliance and increases operational burden.

controls.objective_text: The organization periodically assesses the effectiveness of its AI governance framework through self-assessments, maturity evaluations, and benchmarking against regulatory expectations and peer practices.
controls.implementation_guidance: Conduct annual AI governance self-assessment against the FS AI RMF. Benchmark against regulatory expectations and peer practices. Identify maturity gaps and develop improvement roadmaps. Report assessment results to the board. Consider independent third-party assessments for objectivity.
controls.risk_statement: Without periodic effectiveness assessment, AI governance may not evolve with the pace of AI adoption and regulatory expectations.

controls.objective_text: Lessons learned from regulatory examinations, audit findings, and industry events are systematically incorporated into the AI governance framework.
controls.implementation_guidance: Establish a process to capture and analyze regulatory feedback, audit findings, and industry AI incidents. Assess applicability to the organization's AI program. Prioritize and implement governance framework updates. Track remediation of examination findings with defined timelines. Share learnings across the enterprise.
controls.risk_statement: Failing to incorporate external learnings leads to repeated issues and demonstrates weak continuous improvement to regulators.

controls.objective_text: The organization engages relevant stakeholders — including consumers, community groups, employees, and regulators — in the design and oversight of AI systems that significantly affect them.
controls.implementation_guidance: Identify stakeholder groups affected by each high-risk AI system. Establish feedback mechanisms for consumers (complaint channels, advisory panels). Engage community groups on AI used in lending, particularly in CRA assessment areas. Solicit employee input on AI affecting workplace decisions. Maintain dialogue with examiners on AI plans.
controls.risk_statement: Developing AI without stakeholder engagement risks building systems that fail to meet user needs, exacerbate inequities, or surprise regulators.

controls.objective_text: Consumer feedback and complaint data related to AI-driven decisions are systematically collected, analyzed, and used to improve AI system fairness and performance.
controls.implementation_guidance: Tag consumer complaints related to AI-driven decisions in the complaint management system. Analyze complaint patterns for bias signals and performance issues. Feed complaint insights into model monitoring and retraining processes. Report AI-related complaint trends to governance committee. Comply with CFPB complaint data expectations.
controls.risk_statement: Ignoring consumer feedback on AI-driven decisions perpetuates harmful outcomes and increases CFPB enforcement risk.

controls.objective_text: The organization proactively communicates with prudential regulators about material AI initiatives, seeking supervisory feedback before deployment of high-risk AI systems.
controls.implementation_guidance: Include AI initiatives in regular supervisory discussions. Provide advance notice of material AI deployments (e.g., credit decisioning, BSA/AML). Seek informal feedback on novel AI use cases. Prepare AI briefing materials for examination teams. Maintain a constructive relationship with examiners on AI topics.
controls.risk_statement: Surprising regulators with material AI deployments damages supervisory relationships and increases the likelihood of restrictive MRAs.

controls.objective_text: The organization establishes mechanisms for individuals to contest or appeal AI-driven decisions that materially affect them, including credit decisions, account actions, and employment determinations.
controls.implementation_guidance: Implement appeal processes for AI-driven decisions per regulatory requirements (ECOA adverse action, FCRA dispute rights). Ensure human review of contested AI decisions. Track appeal outcomes and identify patterns suggesting systemic issues. Provide clear instructions to affected individuals on how to exercise appeal rights.
controls.risk_statement: Absence of appeal mechanisms for AI decisions violates consumer protection laws and denies individuals due process rights.

controls.objective_text: Adverse action notices for AI-driven credit decisions comply with ECOA and FCRA requirements, providing specific and accurate reasons for denial that reflect the actual factors in the AI model's decision.
controls.implementation_guidance: Ensure AI-driven adverse action reasons are derived from the model's actual decision factors, not generic templates. Validate that reason codes accurately reflect model behavior through regular testing. Comply with CFPB guidance on AI-specific adverse action requirements. Train compliance staff on AI-specific adverse action challenges.
controls.risk_statement: Inaccurate adverse action notices from AI credit models violate ECOA/FCRA and are a leading source of fair lending enforcement actions.

controls.objective_text: The organization monitors the resolution of contested AI decisions to identify systemic issues and feeds results back into model improvement and governance processes.
controls.implementation_guidance: Track and analyze outcomes of AI decision appeals. Identify patterns such as disproportionate overturns for specific demographic groups. Use appeal data as an input to model fairness monitoring. Escalate systemic findings to model owners and governance committee. Incorporate insights into model retraining where appropriate.
controls.risk_statement: Unanalyzed appeal data represents wasted intelligence on potential model fairness and accuracy issues.

controls.objective_text: The organization maintains a current understanding of AI-related risks to financial stability, operational resilience, and systemic interconnectedness, informed by industry intelligence and supervisory communications.
controls.implementation_guidance: Monitor emerging AI risks through industry groups (e.g., FS-ISAC, CRI, BIS publications), supervisory speeches, and examination feedback. Assess AI concentration risks in critical financial functions. Evaluate potential for correlated AI failures across institutions. Report emerging risk intelligence to the risk committee.
controls.risk_statement: Failure to monitor emerging AI risks leaves the organization unprepared for novel threats and regulatory shifts.

controls.objective_text: AI risk assessments consider macro-level financial stability implications, including the potential for AI-driven herding behavior, flash events, and algorithmic amplification of market stress.
controls.implementation_guidance: Include financial stability considerations in AI risk assessments for trading, market making, and portfolio management AI. Evaluate potential for correlated AI behavior across market participants. Implement circuit breakers and human override mechanisms for AI in market-sensitive functions. Coordinate with prudential supervisors on systemic risk concerns.
controls.risk_statement: AI systems in market-sensitive functions can amplify systemic risk through correlated behavior and speed-of-light decision making.

controls.objective_text: The organization participates in industry forums and information-sharing initiatives related to AI risk management in financial services.
controls.implementation_guidance: Actively participate in CRI FS AI RMF working groups, FS-ISAC AI threat intelligence sharing, and relevant regulatory roundtables. Contribute to and benefit from peer benchmarking on AI governance maturity. Share non-proprietary lessons learned from AI incidents. Engage with standards bodies on AI governance frameworks.
controls.risk_statement: Isolation from industry AI risk intelligence leaves the organization unable to benchmark practices or anticipate emerging regulatory expectations.

controls.objective_text: The organization assesses and manages AI-related risks arising from third-party AI providers, including concentration risk from dependence on a small number of foundation model providers.
controls.implementation_guidance: Inventory all third-party AI dependencies. Assess concentration risk from reliance on major cloud AI and foundation model providers. Develop contingency plans for provider disruption. Include AI-specific provisions in vendor contracts. Monitor provider financial health, security posture, and model change practices.
controls.risk_statement: Concentration in a few AI providers creates systemic dependency that could simultaneously disrupt multiple financial institutions.

controls.objective_text: Third-party AI vendor risk assessments include evaluation of the vendor's own AI governance practices, model development standards, and ability to support the institution's regulatory obligations.
controls.implementation_guidance: Develop AI-specific vendor due diligence questionnaires. Evaluate vendor AI governance maturity, development practices, testing, and monitoring capabilities. Assess vendor ability to provide model documentation, performance data, and validation support. Include right-to-audit clauses for AI components. Review vendor AI practices at least annually.
controls.risk_statement: Vendors with weak AI governance practices transfer unmanaged model risk to the financial institution, which remains accountable to regulators.

controls.objective_text: Contracts with AI vendors include provisions for model transparency, performance reporting, incident notification, data handling, and regulatory examination access.
controls.implementation_guidance: Negotiate contractual provisions requiring: model documentation disclosure, regular performance reports, prompt incident notification, data handling per institutional standards, and examination access per OCC/Fed expectations. Include provisions for model change notification and approval. Address data ownership and return upon contract termination.
controls.risk_statement: Inadequate contractual provisions limit the institution's ability to validate, monitor, and demonstrate governance over vendor AI models.

controls.objective_text: For each proposed AI use case, the organization documents the intended purpose, scope, target population, expected benefits, and potential risks in a structured use case assessment.
controls.implementation_guidance: Create a standardized AI use case assessment template. Require completion before development begins. Include: business problem, proposed AI approach, target population (with demographic analysis), expected benefits (quantified), potential risks, regulatory implications, and alignment with AI strategy. Review and approve through governance process.
controls.risk_statement: Deploying AI without clear purpose documentation leads to scope creep, unintended uses, and inability to demonstrate AI system intent to regulators.

controls.objective_text: Use case assessments for consumer-facing AI include analysis of potential disparate impact on protected classes and underserved populations, including communities identified in CRA assessments.
controls.implementation_guidance: Require pre-deployment disparate impact analysis for AI affecting consumers. Evaluate potential effects across race, gender, age, national origin, and other protected characteristics. Consider impact on underserved populations and CRA assessment areas. Document analysis methodology and findings. Obtain fair lending compliance sign-off before proceeding.
controls.risk_statement: AI deployed without disparate impact analysis may perpetuate or amplify discrimination, resulting in fair lending violations and enforcement actions.

controls.objective_text: The organization evaluates whether AI is the appropriate solution for each proposed use case, considering alternatives such as traditional statistical models, rules-based systems, or human processes.
controls.implementation_guidance: Require justification for AI over simpler alternatives. Evaluate whether traditional approaches achieve acceptable performance. Document the incremental benefit of AI versus the additional complexity and risk. Consider explainability requirements — high-explainability needs may favor simpler models. Include cost-benefit analysis in the assessment.
controls.risk_statement: Deploying AI where simpler methods suffice unnecessarily increases model risk, complexity, and governance burden without commensurate benefit.

controls.objective_text: The organization identifies and documents all stakeholders affected by each AI system, including internal users, consumers, regulators, and third parties, and assesses the nature and magnitude of impact on each group.
controls.implementation_guidance: Map stakeholders for each AI system using a structured stakeholder analysis. Categorize by type: direct users, decision subjects, oversight functions, regulators, and ecosystem participants. Assess magnitude of impact (financial, access, privacy, employment). Prioritize high-impact stakeholder groups for engagement and risk mitigation.
controls.risk_statement: Incomplete stakeholder identification leads to overlooked impacts, unaddressed risks, and surprised regulators or consumers.

controls.objective_text: Stakeholder analysis includes specific assessment of consumer impact for AI used in credit, deposit, payment, insurance, and investment products, with particular attention to financially vulnerable populations.
controls.implementation_guidance: Conduct consumer impact assessments for AI in financial products. Analyze effects on credit access, pricing, account management, and service quality. Evaluate impact on LMI borrowers, elderly consumers, LEP individuals, and other vulnerable populations. Align with CFPB guidance on algorithmic harm. Document consumer-specific risk mitigations.
controls.risk_statement: AI in financial products that harms vulnerable consumers creates acute regulatory, legal, and reputational risk for the institution.

controls.objective_text: Stakeholder engagement findings are documented and integrated into AI system design decisions, with traceability from stakeholder input to system requirements.
controls.implementation_guidance: Maintain records of stakeholder engagement activities and findings. Create traceability matrices linking stakeholder feedback to design decisions. Document where stakeholder input changed system design versus where it was noted but not incorporated (with justification). Review traceability during validation and audits.
controls.risk_statement: Stakeholder engagement without integration into design is performative and does not reduce actual risk to affected populations.

controls.objective_text: The organization defines measurable performance requirements for each AI system, including accuracy, precision, recall, latency, and business-specific metrics, prior to development.
controls.implementation_guidance: Establish quantitative performance requirements during use case approval. Include statistical metrics (accuracy, AUC, precision, recall) and business metrics (dollar impact, processing time, customer satisfaction). Define minimum acceptable thresholds and target performance levels. Document requirements in model development documentation per SR 11-7.
controls.risk_statement: AI systems developed without predefined performance requirements cannot be objectively evaluated, leading to subjective go/no-go decisions.

controls.objective_text: Performance requirements include fairness metrics with quantitative thresholds, defined for relevant protected class attributes and aligned with fair lending and anti-discrimination requirements.
controls.implementation_guidance: Define fairness metrics appropriate to the use case (e.g., demographic parity, equalized odds, predictive parity). Set quantitative thresholds for acceptable disparity ratios. Require fairness testing across race, gender, age, and other protected characteristics. Align with CFPB and DOJ expectations for fair lending analytics. Document methodology and thresholds.
controls.risk_statement: AI systems without quantitative fairness requirements may pass accuracy tests while producing discriminatory outcomes that trigger enforcement action.

controls.objective_text: Performance requirements include robustness criteria, specifying acceptable performance degradation under stressed conditions, distribution shift, and adversarial scenarios relevant to financial services.
controls.implementation_guidance: Define robustness requirements including performance under economic stress scenarios (recession, rate shock), data quality degradation, and adversarial manipulation. Specify maximum acceptable performance degradation percentages. Align stress scenarios with enterprise stress testing frameworks (CCAR/DFAST where applicable). Test robustness during validation.
controls.risk_statement: AI systems that perform well in normal conditions but fail under stress create procyclical risk that amplifies financial downturns.

controls.objective_text: The organization identifies and documents risks specific to each AI system, including data risks, model risks, operational risks, and compliance risks, using a structured risk identification methodology.
controls.implementation_guidance: Conduct system-specific risk identification workshops with cross-functional participation (business, technology, risk, compliance). Use structured methodologies such as risk taxonomies, failure mode analysis, or threat modeling. Document identified risks with likelihood, impact, and proposed mitigations. Maintain a risk register for each AI system.
controls.risk_statement: Generic risk assessments miss system-specific risks, leaving unique threat vectors unmitigated.

controls.objective_text: AI risk identification explicitly addresses risks unique to AI/ML systems, including concept drift, data poisoning, adversarial attacks, model extraction, and emergent behaviors in complex models.
controls.implementation_guidance: Include AI-specific risk categories in the risk identification process. Assess: concept and data drift, training data poisoning, adversarial manipulation, model theft/extraction, unexpected emergent behaviors (especially in deep learning and foundation models), and hallucination risk (for generative AI). Map each risk to monitoring and control strategies.
controls.risk_statement: Traditional risk identification approaches miss novel AI-specific threats, leaving organizations vulnerable to risks unique to machine learning systems.

controls.objective_text: Risk identification for AI in financial services includes assessment of risks to financial inclusion, equitable access, and potential for digital redlining or algorithmic exclusion.
controls.implementation_guidance: Evaluate AI systems for potential to create or reinforce barriers to financial access. Assess whether AI-driven eligibility, pricing, or servicing decisions could produce digital redlining effects. Analyze geographic and demographic patterns in AI outcomes. Engage CRA and fair lending officers in risk identification for relevant AI systems.
controls.risk_statement: AI-driven financial exclusion constitutes a modern form of redlining, with severe fair lending, CRA, and reputational consequences.

controls.objective_text: The organization assesses and documents the potential financial, operational, reputational, and consumer impact of AI system failures or adverse outcomes, using quantitative analysis where feasible.
controls.implementation_guidance: Conduct impact assessments for AI system failure scenarios. Quantify potential financial losses (direct and indirect). Assess operational disruption to business lines and customers. Evaluate reputational impact and potential media scrutiny. Estimate consumer harm in terms of affected population size and severity. Use scenario analysis aligned with enterprise stress testing.
controls.risk_statement: Underestimating AI failure impact leads to insufficient controls and inadequate contingency planning for high-consequence events.

controls.objective_text: Impact assessments for AI systems in critical banking functions (payments, clearing, settlement) consider cascading effects on counterparties, market participants, and financial system stability.
controls.implementation_guidance: For AI in systemically important functions, extend impact analysis beyond the institution. Map downstream dependencies and counterparty exposures. Assess potential for cascading failures through payment networks, clearing houses, and correspondent banking relationships. Coordinate with treasury, operations, and market risk functions. Consider SIFMU interconnections.
controls.risk_statement: AI failures in critical banking infrastructure can propagate through the financial system, creating systemic risk beyond the originating institution.

controls.objective_text: Impact assessment results are used to determine control intensity, monitoring frequency, and business continuity requirements proportionate to the assessed risk.
controls.implementation_guidance: Link impact assessment results to control requirements. Higher-impact AI systems receive more intensive validation, more frequent monitoring, and more robust fallback procedures. Document the rationale connecting impact assessment to control design. Review impact assessments annually or after material changes to the AI system or its operating environment.
controls.risk_statement: Impact assessments that do not drive proportionate controls provide false assurance without reducing actual risk.

controls.objective_text: The organization evaluates and documents the benefits, costs, and risks of AI systems compared to non-AI alternatives and the status quo, supporting informed go/no-go decisions.
controls.implementation_guidance: Require business case documentation that compares AI to alternatives. Quantify incremental benefit of AI (accuracy improvement, cost reduction, speed gain). Assess incremental risk and governance cost. Document the decision rationale. Require sign-off from business and risk leadership. Reassess periodically as AI performance data accumulates.
controls.risk_statement: Deploying AI without rigorous cost-benefit analysis may result in investments that increase risk without proportionate business value.

controls.objective_text: Cost-benefit analysis includes the total cost of AI governance, including validation, monitoring, regulatory compliance, and potential remediation costs, not solely development and operational costs.
controls.implementation_guidance: Include full lifecycle governance costs in AI business cases. Account for: validation resources, ongoing monitoring, regulatory examination support, documentation maintenance, retraining costs, and potential remediation/incident response costs. Use historical data from existing AI systems to improve cost estimates. Update estimates as governance requirements evolve.
controls.risk_statement: Underestimating AI governance costs leads to under-resourced oversight and may make unprofitable AI systems appear viable.

controls.objective_text: The organization establishes criteria for discontinuing AI systems that no longer provide sufficient benefit relative to their risk and governance cost.
controls.implementation_guidance: Define trigger criteria for AI system decommissioning review (e.g., declining performance, increasing maintenance cost, regulatory changes, superseding technology). Require periodic value realization reviews for all AI systems. Establish a decommissioning process including data retention, model archival, and transition planning. Ensure decommissioned models are removed from the active inventory.
controls.risk_statement: Legacy AI systems that persist without value realization consume governance resources and may accumulate unmonitored risk.

controls.objective_text: The organization defines and validates the target operating environment for each AI system, including data inputs, integration points, user populations, and decision contexts in which the model will operate.
controls.implementation_guidance: Document the intended operating environment comprehensively: data sources and their characteristics, upstream and downstream system integrations, user populations and their technical capabilities, decision contexts and time constraints. Validate that the operating environment matches development assumptions. Monitor for environmental changes post-deployment.
controls.risk_statement: AI systems deployed in environments that differ from development assumptions may produce unexpected and unreliable results.

controls.objective_text: The organization assesses how AI system outputs will be used in human decision-making processes, including the degree of human reliance, automation level, and override capabilities.
controls.implementation_guidance: Document the human-AI interaction model for each system. Specify whether AI output is advisory, augmenting, or autonomous. Define human override capabilities and when they should be exercised. Assess the risk of automation bias — humans over-relying on AI recommendations. Design user interfaces to support appropriate skepticism. Test human-AI decision quality jointly.
controls.risk_statement: Poorly designed human-AI interaction leads to automation bias or disuse, negating the intended benefits of AI augmentation.

controls.objective_text: For AI used in real-time transaction processing (payments, trading, fraud detection), the operating environment assessment includes latency requirements, throughput capacity, and failover procedures.
controls.implementation_guidance: Define performance SLAs for real-time AI systems including maximum latency, minimum throughput, and availability targets. Test under peak load conditions. Implement graceful degradation and fallback to rules-based processing. Define automated and manual failover procedures. Align with enterprise business continuity and disaster recovery standards.
controls.risk_statement: Real-time AI systems that fail to meet performance requirements in production can disrupt critical financial services and harm consumers.

controls.objective_text: The organization maps and documents the complete AI system architecture, including data pipelines, model components, feature engineering, inference services, and monitoring infrastructure.
controls.implementation_guidance: Create comprehensive architecture documentation for each AI system. Include data flow diagrams from source to prediction. Document all model components, feature transformations, and inference pathways. Map dependencies on shared infrastructure and services. Maintain architecture diagrams as living documents updated with each change.
controls.risk_statement: Undocumented AI architecture creates operational risk, impedes troubleshooting, and prevents effective validation and audit.

controls.objective_text: System mapping identifies all dependencies on external data sources, APIs, and third-party services, with contingency plans for dependency failures.
controls.implementation_guidance: Catalog all external dependencies for each AI system. Assess reliability and SLAs of each dependency. Develop contingency responses for dependency failures (fallback data sources, cached models, degraded mode operations). Test dependency failure scenarios regularly. Monitor dependency health in real-time.
controls.risk_statement: Unmapped external dependencies create single points of failure that can cascade to AI system outages without warning.

controls.objective_text: Architecture documentation is maintained at sufficient detail to support regulatory examination, independent validation, and disaster recovery for the AI system.
controls.implementation_guidance: Ensure documentation supports three use cases: examination (regulators can understand system design), validation (independent reviewers can assess appropriateness), and DR (operations can rebuild/restore). Version-control documentation alongside code. Include deployment configurations, environment specifications, and recovery procedures.
controls.risk_statement: Architecture documentation that cannot support examination, validation, or recovery is insufficient for a regulated financial institution.

controls.objective_text: The organization identifies and assesses AI-specific scientific and technical limitations for each system, including model uncertainty, known failure modes, and conditions under which the model should not be relied upon.
controls.implementation_guidance: Document known limitations for each AI system. Include: model assumptions and where they break down, data conditions causing unreliable predictions, populations or scenarios where performance is degraded, uncertainty quantification and confidence intervals. Communicate limitations to users and decision-makers. Include limitations in model documentation per SR 11-7.
controls.risk_statement: Users unaware of AI system limitations may rely on outputs in inappropriate contexts, leading to poor decisions and consumer harm.

controls.objective_text: Technical limitations assessment addresses the explainability constraints of the chosen modeling approach, particularly for complex models used in consumer-facing decisions subject to adverse action requirements.
controls.implementation_guidance: Evaluate explainability constraints for each model type. For complex models (deep learning, ensemble methods), assess whether model-agnostic explanation methods (SHAP, LIME) provide sufficient fidelity for regulatory requirements. Document explainability methodology and its limitations. For credit models, validate that explanation methods produce adverse action reasons consistent with model behavior.
controls.risk_statement: Using models whose decisions cannot be adequately explained in consumer-facing credit decisions violates ECOA and FCRA requirements.

controls.objective_text: Limitations assessments for generative AI systems address hallucination risk, factual accuracy constraints, training data cutoff dates, and potential for generating harmful or non-compliant content.
controls.implementation_guidance: For generative AI systems, conduct specific limitations assessments covering: hallucination rates by content type, factual accuracy limitations, training data recency and gaps, potential for generating biased or harmful content, and susceptibility to prompt injection. Implement guardrails proportionate to identified limitations. Document residual risks accepted.
controls.risk_statement: Generative AI deployed in financial services without limitations assessment risks producing inaccurate financial information, misleading advice, or non-compliant content.

controls.objective_text: The organization establishes and enforces data quality standards for AI training, validation, and production data, including completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, and representativeness requirements.
controls.implementation_guidance: Define quantitative data quality metrics and thresholds for AI data. Implement automated data quality checks in data pipelines. Monitor data quality continuously for production AI systems. Establish data quality incident processes. Align with enterprise data governance standards. Document data quality assessment results in model documentation.
controls.risk_statement: Poor data quality is the leading cause of AI model failures and a persistent examination finding in model risk management reviews.

controls.objective_text: Data used in AI systems is assessed for representativeness relative to the target population, with specific analysis of whether historically underserved populations are adequately represented.
controls.implementation_guidance: Analyze training data composition across demographic dimensions. Identify underrepresented populations and assess impact on model performance for those groups. Evaluate whether historical data reflects past discriminatory practices that could bias the model. Implement data augmentation or reweighting strategies where appropriate. Document representativeness analysis in model documentation.
controls.risk_statement: Unrepresentative training data produces models that perform poorly for underserved populations, perpetuating historical inequities in financial services.

controls.objective_text: Data lineage is documented end-to-end for AI systems, tracing data from source through transformation to model input, supporting auditability and regulatory examination.
controls.implementation_guidance: Implement data lineage tracking for AI data pipelines. Document: original data sources, collection methods, transformation logic, feature engineering steps, and final model input specifications. Use automated lineage tools where feasible. Ensure lineage documentation is sufficient for independent reproduction. Review lineage accuracy during validation.
controls.risk_statement: Without data lineage, the organization cannot trace model inputs to sources, impeding validation, audit, and incident investigation.

controls.objective_text: The organization evaluates and documents the provenance and licensing of third-party and publicly sourced data used in AI systems, ensuring compliance with data usage rights and privacy regulations.
controls.implementation_guidance: Maintain a data provenance registry for AI data sources. Verify licensing and usage rights for third-party data. Assess privacy compliance for data used in AI (CCPA, GLBA, state privacy laws). Evaluate ethical considerations of data sourcing. Document provenance in model documentation. Review data usage rights annually or upon contract renewal.
controls.risk_statement: Using data without proper licensing or in violation of privacy regulations exposes the institution to legal liability and regulatory action.

controls.objective_text: The organization assesses AI training and operational data for embedded biases, including historical discrimination patterns, sampling biases, and proxy variable effects.
controls.implementation_guidance: Conduct systematic bias assessment for AI training data. Test for: correlation between features and protected characteristics (proxy analysis), historical patterns reflecting discriminatory practices (e.g., redlining in mortgage data), sampling biases that underrepresent populations, and labeling biases in supervised learning data. Document findings and remediation strategies.
controls.risk_statement: Biased training data produces biased AI outputs — a primary mechanism for algorithmic discrimination in financial services.

controls.objective_text: For AI used in credit decisioning, the organization evaluates all input features for potential proxy discrimination, particularly features correlated with race, ethnicity, national origin, or other protected characteristics.
controls.implementation_guidance: Conduct proxy variable analysis for all credit model features. Quantify correlation between each feature and protected characteristics. Evaluate whether proxy features provide legitimate predictive value versus merely encoding protected class information. Consult with fair lending compliance and legal on borderline features. Document analysis and feature selection rationale.
controls.risk_statement: Features that proxy for protected characteristics in credit models create disparate impact liability and are a primary focus of CFPB and DOJ fair lending examinations.

controls.objective_text: Data bias assessment methodologies and findings are reviewed by independent model risk management and fair lending compliance functions before model approval.
controls.implementation_guidance: Require second-line review of data bias assessments. MRM validates methodology and technical rigor. Fair lending compliance evaluates regulatory implications of findings. Joint sign-off required before model can proceed through development gates. Document review findings and any conditions imposed. Escalate unresolved disagreements to governance committee.
controls.risk_statement: First-line bias assessments without independent review may underestimate bias risk due to confirmation bias or insufficient fair lending expertise.

controls.objective_text: The organization classifies AI-related data according to its sensitivity and applies data protection controls commensurate with classification, including encryption, access controls, and retention policies.
controls.implementation_guidance: Apply enterprise data classification standards to AI data. Classify training data, model parameters, feature stores, and inference logs by sensitivity level. Implement encryption at rest and in transit for sensitive AI data. Enforce least-privilege access controls. Define retention and disposal policies per regulatory requirements (GLBA, state laws). Secure model artifacts as confidential.
controls.risk_statement: AI data that is unclassified or under-protected creates privacy and security risks, potentially violating GLBA, CCPA, and other data protection requirements.

controls.objective_text: AI systems that process personally identifiable information (PII) or nonpublic personal information (NPI) implement privacy-preserving techniques and comply with applicable privacy regulations.
controls.implementation_guidance: Inventory PII/NPI usage across AI systems. Implement data minimization — use only PII necessary for the AI purpose. Apply privacy-preserving techniques where feasible (anonymization, pseudonymization, differential privacy, federated learning). Ensure compliance with GLBA, CCPA/CPRA, and state privacy laws. Conduct privacy impact assessments for AI systems processing sensitive data.
controls.risk_statement: AI systems processing PII without privacy controls risk data breaches, regulatory penalties, and erosion of consumer trust.

controls.objective_text: Controls prevent AI training data and model outputs from being inadvertently exposed through model inversion, membership inference, or data extraction attacks.
controls.implementation_guidance: Assess AI systems for data leakage vulnerabilities. Implement controls against: model inversion attacks (reconstructing training data from model outputs), membership inference attacks (determining if specific data was in training set), and data extraction from generative AI. Apply output perturbation, access rate limiting, and monitoring for anomalous query patterns.
controls.risk_statement: AI models that leak training data through inference expose sensitive financial and personal information, violating privacy obligations.

controls.objective_text: The organization evaluates the suitability and limitations of AI training data relative to the intended use case, including temporal relevance, geographic coverage, and domain applicability.
controls.implementation_guidance: Assess training data fitness for the specific AI use case. Evaluate temporal coverage — ensure data spans relevant economic cycles for financial models. Assess geographic relevance to the institution's market footprint. Verify domain applicability (e.g., retail banking data for retail banking AI). Document data suitability assessment and residual limitations.
controls.risk_statement: Training data unsuitable for the use case produces unreliable models that may fail unpredictably when encountering real-world conditions.

controls.objective_text: For credit risk AI models, training data includes representation across economic cycles (expansion, contraction, recovery) to ensure model robustness through varying macroeconomic conditions.
controls.implementation_guidance: Ensure credit model training data spans at least one full economic cycle. Include stress period data (e.g., 2008-2009, COVID-2020). Assess model sensitivity to macroeconomic conditions through scenario analysis. Supplement limited-period data with synthetic stress scenarios where necessary. Align with CCAR/DFAST stress testing data standards.
controls.risk_statement: Credit AI models trained only on benign economic data fail during downturns, precisely when accurate risk assessment is most critical.

controls.objective_text: Data suitability assessment for AI includes evaluation of label quality for supervised learning, ensuring labels are accurate, consistent, and free from systematic bias.
controls.implementation_guidance: Assess label quality for supervised learning AI systems. Evaluate labeling methodology and quality control processes. Test for inter-rater reliability where human labeling is used. Identify potential label biases (e.g., historical approval bias in credit data, investigation bias in fraud labels). Document label quality assessment and known limitations.
controls.risk_statement: Poor label quality silently corrupts supervised learning models, producing systematically biased outputs that appear technically valid.

controls.objective_text: The organization establishes data governance processes specific to AI, including data access approval, usage tracking, and compliance with data usage agreements for AI training and inference.
controls.implementation_guidance: Extend enterprise data governance to address AI-specific needs. Implement AI data access approval workflows. Track data usage across AI systems to ensure compliance with usage agreements and regulatory requirements. Maintain data usage logs for audit purposes. Coordinate with data stewards and data owners on AI data requests.
controls.risk_statement: Ungoverned AI data usage risks violating data usage agreements, privacy regulations, and internal data governance standards.

controls.objective_text: Data retention and disposal for AI systems complies with regulatory record-keeping requirements while managing storage costs and privacy obligations.
controls.implementation_guidance: Define AI data retention policies aligned with regulatory requirements (7-year minimum for many banking records). Address retention of training data, model artifacts, inference logs, and monitoring data. Implement secure disposal processes for expired AI data. Balance retention requirements with privacy obligations (right to deletion). Document retention schedules in model documentation.
controls.risk_statement: Improper data retention or premature disposal may violate banking record-keeping requirements or impede regulatory examination.

controls.objective_text: Feature stores and shared data assets used across multiple AI systems are governed with version control, access management, and impact analysis capabilities.
controls.implementation_guidance: Implement governance for shared AI data assets (feature stores, embeddings, reference data). Enforce version control for feature definitions. Maintain access controls and usage logging. Conduct impact analysis before modifying shared features to assess downstream effects on dependent AI systems. Establish change management processes for shared data assets.
controls.risk_statement: Ungoverned shared data assets create hidden dependencies where changes to one feature can silently degrade multiple AI systems.

controls.objective_text: The organization maps AI systems to specific business processes and decisions they support, maintaining traceability from AI output to business action.
controls.implementation_guidance: Create a mapping of AI systems to business processes, decisions, and products they support. Document the role of AI in each decision (advisory, augmenting, autonomous). Maintain traceability from AI predictions to downstream business actions. Enable analysis of business impact when AI systems change or fail. Update mappings when AI system use expands.
controls.risk_statement: Without clear mapping of AI to business processes, the organization cannot assess the full impact of AI changes or failures on operations.

controls.objective_text: Business process owners are engaged in AI system design and monitoring to ensure AI outputs align with business intent and regulatory requirements for the processes they support.
controls.implementation_guidance: Require business process owner involvement throughout the AI lifecycle. Business owners validate that AI outputs align with business intent. Include business owners in monitoring review and threshold-setting. Ensure business owners understand AI system limitations and failure modes. Define business owner responsibilities in the RACI for each AI system.
controls.risk_statement: AI systems developed without business process owner engagement may produce technically correct outputs that are operationally inappropriate or misaligned with business goals.

controls.objective_text: For AI embedded in regulatory compliance processes (BSA/AML, sanctions screening, fair lending monitoring), the mapping includes specific regulatory requirements the AI supports and how compliance is verified.
controls.implementation_guidance: Document the regulatory requirements addressed by AI in compliance processes. Map AI capabilities to specific regulatory obligations (e.g., BSA suspicious activity detection, OFAC sanctions screening, HMDA fair lending analysis). Define how AI contributions to compliance are validated. Ensure compliance officers can explain AI role to examiners. Maintain fallback compliance processes.
controls.risk_statement: AI in compliance processes that fails silently or is poorly understood by compliance staff creates regulatory compliance risk.

controls.objective_text: The organization assesses and documents the degree of human oversight and intervention capability for each AI system, ensuring appropriate human-in-the-loop or human-on-the-loop controls based on risk level.
controls.implementation_guidance: Define the human oversight model for each AI system (human-in-the-loop, human-on-the-loop, or human-in-command). Align oversight level with risk tier — higher risk requires more direct human involvement. Ensure human reviewers have sufficient expertise and information to exercise meaningful oversight. Test override mechanisms regularly. Document oversight model in model documentation.
controls.risk_statement: Insufficient human oversight of AI allows errors to propagate undetected, while excessive oversight negates AI efficiency benefits.

controls.objective_text: Human override capabilities are implemented and tested for all high-risk AI systems, with kill switches or circuit breakers that can halt AI processing in emergency situations.
controls.implementation_guidance: Implement kill switch capabilities for all high-risk AI systems. Test override mechanisms under realistic conditions, including high-volume scenarios. Define clear procedures for when and how to invoke overrides. Ensure override capabilities are accessible to authorized personnel 24/7. Log all override events for post-incident review. Practice override procedures in business continuity exercises.
controls.risk_statement: High-risk AI systems without tested override capabilities cannot be safely halted during adverse events, potentially amplifying harm.

controls.objective_text: The organization monitors the quality and consistency of human oversight decisions to detect automation bias, alert fatigue, and degradation in human review effectiveness.
controls.implementation_guidance: Track metrics on human oversight quality: override rates, review times, consistency across reviewers, and agreement with AI recommendations. Monitor for automation bias signals (rubber-stamping AI outputs). Address alert fatigue by optimizing AI system thresholds to reduce false positives. Provide periodic training to human reviewers. Rotate reviewers to prevent complacency.
controls.risk_statement: Human oversight that degrades into rubber-stamping provides false assurance while offering no actual risk mitigation.
